bw: Cardiac muscle starts its own electrical impulse at a fixed rate
Neither smooth nor skeletal muscle can do this
tp: Heart rate is modulated by the endocrine and nervous systems, but the heart’s ability to start its own impulses is autorhythmicity.

ww.Tetany: Tetany is sustained involuntary contraction, which the heart avoids.
ww.Summation: Summation is the adding of twitches in skeletal muscle and is not the heart’s self-starting property.

evidence: This property is known as autorhythmicity.

bw: Junction between adjoining cardiac muscle cells
tp: Gap junctions at intercalated discs pass ions between cells and help synchronize contraction; desmosomes bear the force.

ww.Z disc: A Z disc marks the boundary of a sarcomere inside one cell.
ww.Motor end plate: A motor end plate is the neuromuscular junction of skeletal muscle.

evidence: A junction between two adjoining cells is marked by a critical structure called an intercalated disc, which helps support the synchronized contraction of the muscle (Figure 19.17b).

d: At the junction of the A and I bands
tp: Because cardiac T tubules sit only at Z discs, there are half as many as in skeletal muscle, where they lie at the A-I junction.

ww.At the junction of the A and I bands: That is where T tubules lie in skeletal muscle.
ww.At the M line: T tubules are not at the M line in either muscle type.

evidence: The T tubules are only found at the Z discs, whereas in skeletal muscle, they are found at the junction of the A and I bands.

bw: Share supplied by Ca2+ influx during the plateau phase
tp: Plateau-phase Ca2+ influx supplies about 20 percent of contraction calcium; the rest is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

ww.About 80 percent: About 80 percent is the share released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
ww.About 50 percent: The source gives about 20 percent for influx, not half.

evidence: Approximately 20 percent of the calcium required for contraction is supplied by the influx of Ca2+ during the plateau phase.

bw: Superior and posterior wall of the right atrium
tp: The SA node initiates the sinus rhythm; the other conduction components have progressively slower inherent rates.

ww.Atrioventricular (AV) node: The AV node is a second, slower clump in the atrioventricular septum.
ww.Bundle of His: The bundle of His carries the impulse from the AV node through the interventricular septum.

evidence: The SA node has the highest inherent rate of depolarization and is known as the pacemaker of the heart.

tp: Rates fall progressively along the conduction system: SA node 80–100, AV node 40–60, AV bundle 30–40, bundle branches 20–30, Purkinje fibers 15–20 per minute.

ww.40–60 beats per minute: That is the inherent rate of the AV node.
ww.15–20 beats per minute: That is the inherent rate of the Purkinje fibers.

evidence: The SA node, without nervous or endocrine control, would initiate a heart impulse approximately 80–100 times per minute.

tp: Even with total SA block, the AV node continues contractions at 40–60 per minute, enough to maintain consciousness.

ww.80–100 beats per minute: That is the SA node’s inherent rate.
ww.15–20 beats per minute: That is the Purkinje fibers’ inherent rate.

evidence: Without the SA node, the AV node would generate a heart rate of 40–60 beats per minute.

bw: Inherent firing rate of the Purkinje fibers
tp: The inherent rate gets slower as you move from the SA node to the Purkinje fibers.

ww.30–40 impulses per minute: That is the inherent rate of the atrioventricular bundle.
ww.20–30 impulses per minute: That is the inherent rate of the bundle branches.

evidence: The bundle branches would have an inherent rate of 20–30 impulses per minute, and the Purkinje fibers would fire at 15–20 impulses per minute.

bw: About 100 ms pause before the impulse passes on
ans: Lets the atria finish contracting before the ventricles are stimulated
d: Lets the ventricles fill by passive flow only
Stops the SA node firing too quickly
tp: The delay comes partly from the small diameter of nodal cells and inefficient conduction between them.

ww.Lets the ventricles fill by passive flow: The delay lets the atria add their pumped volume before the ventricles contract.
ww.Stops the SA node firing too quickly: The delay acts after the SA node, on the impulse reaching the ventricles.

evidence: This pause is critical to heart function, as it allows the atrial cardiomyocytes to complete their contraction that pumps blood into the ventricles before the impulse is transmitted to the cells of the ventricle itself.

bw: AV node under extreme SA node stimulation
Sets the typical maximum heart rate in a healthy young person
tp: Damaged or drug-stimulated hearts can beat faster, but then they can no longer pump blood effectively.

ww.120 per minute: The AV node can transmit impulses well above 120 per minute.
ww.350 per minute: The AV node limit is 220 per minute in a healthy young person.

evidence: With extreme stimulation by the SA node, the AV node can transmit impulses maximally at 220 per minute.

bw: Divides into left and right bundle branches
tp: The left bundle branch is larger than the right because the left ventricle is larger.

ww.Purkinje fibers: Purkinje fibers are the terminal fibers that spread the impulse from the apex through the ventricular muscle.
ww.Bachmann’s bundle: Bachmann’s bundle is the interatrial band between the right and left atria.

evidence: Arising from the AV node, the atrioventricular bundle, or bundle of His, proceeds through the interventricular septum before dividing into two atrioventricular bundle branches, commonly called the left and right bundle branches.

bw: Conducts the impulse directly from the right atrium to the left atrium
tp: Bachmann’s bundle carries the impulse across the atria in addition to the internodal pathways.

ww.Bundle of His: The bundle of His runs from the AV node into the interventricular septum.
ww.Moderator band: Part of the right bundle branch runs in the moderator band, which supplies the right papillary muscles.

evidence: In addition, there is a specialized pathway called Bachmann’s bundle or the interatrial band that conducts the impulse directly from the right atrium to the left atrium.

bw: Like squeezing a tube of toothpaste from the bottom
ans: Ventricular contraction begins at the apex and travels toward the base
d: Ventricular contraction begins at the base and travels toward the apex
Both ventricles contract from the septum outward
tp: Apex-to-base contraction drives blood out of the ventricles into the aorta and pulmonary trunk.

ww.Ventricular contraction begins at the ba: The stimulus begins at the apex, so contraction does too.
ww.Both ventricles contract from the septum: The source describes an apex-to-base sequence, not septum outward.

evidence: Since the electrical stimulus begins at the apex, the contraction also begins at the apex and travels toward the base of the heart, similar to squeezing a tube of toothpaste from the bottom.

bw: Slow rise in membrane potential from −60 mV to about −40 mV
tp: Conductive cells have no stable resting potential; slow sodium influx creates spontaneous depolarization, then calcium enters and K+ leaves for repolarization.

ww.Calcium (Ca2+) influx: Calcium channels open later, at about −40 mV, for the faster rise.
ww.Potassium (K+) efflux: K+ efflux causes repolarization, not the slow initial rise.

evidence: Conductive cells contain a series of sodium ion channels that allow a normal and slow influx of sodium ions that causes the membrane potential to rise slowly from an initial value of −60 mV up to about –40 mV.

bw: Faster depolarization up to about +15 mV
tp: After the calcium channels close, K+ channels open and K+ leaves, causing repolarization.

ww.Opening of potassium channels: K+ channels open later and cause repolarization.
ww.Closing of all sodium channels: The faster rise is due to Ca2+ entry, not closing of sodium channels.

evidence: At this point, calcium ion channels open and Ca2+ enters the cell, further depolarizing it at a more rapid rate until it reaches a value of approximately +15 mV.

ans: Ca2+ entering through slow calcium channels
d: Na+ entering through fast sodium channels
tp: The plateau helps give the long refractory period needed for effective pumping.

ww.Na+ entering through fast sodium channel: Fast sodium channels cause the rapid depolarization before the plateau.
ww.Cl- leaving through chloride channels: The source attributes the plateau to Ca2+ entry with few K+ channels open.

evidence: This is due in large part to the opening of the slow Ca2+ channels, allowing Ca2+ to enter the cell while few K+ channels are open, allowing K+ to exit the cell.

bw: Prevented in the heart by a very long refractory period
tp: Tetany is not compatible with life in the heart because it would stop the pumping of blood.

ww.Fibrillation: Fibrillation is uncoordinated beating, not a sustained contraction.
ww.Autorhythmicity: Autorhythmicity is the heart’s self-starting property.

evidence: The refractory period is very long to prevent the possibility of tetany, a condition in which muscle remains involuntarily contracted.

tp: The atria begin contracting about 25 ms after the start of the P wave.

ww.QRS complex: The QRS complex is ventricular depolarization.
ww.T wave: The T wave is ventricular repolarization.

evidence: The small P wave represents the depolarization of the atria.

tp: The QRS is large because the ventricular muscle is larger and needs a stronger electrical signal. Atrial repolarization occurs during it.

ww.P wave: The P wave is atrial depolarization.
ww.T wave: The T wave is ventricular repolarization.

evidence: The large QRS complex represents the depolarization of the ventricles, which requires a much stronger electrical signal because of the larger size of the ventricular cardiac muscle.

tp: T waves often appear flatter when insufficient oxygen is being delivered to the myocardium.

ww.P wave: The P wave is atrial depolarization.
ww.QRS complex: The QRS complex is ventricular depolarization.

evidence: Lastly, the T wave represents the repolarization of the ventricles.

bw: Delay in conduction between the SA and AV nodes
d: P waves not followed by a QRS complex
No relationship between P waves and QRS complexes
tp: The PR interval measures the time from the start of atrial depolarization to the start of the QRS complex.

ww.P waves not followed by a QRS complex: That pattern is a second-degree (incomplete) block.
ww.No relationship between P waves and QRS: That pattern is a third-degree (complete) block.

evidence: This can be recognized on the ECG as an abnormally long PR interval.

bw: Some impulses from the SA node reach the AV node and others do not
ECG: some P waves are not followed by a QRS complex
tp: In a second-degree block the ECG shows some P waves not followed by a QRS complex while others look normal.

ww.First-degree (partial) AV block: A first-degree block delays every impulse but all get through.
ww.Third-degree (complete) AV block: In a third-degree block no impulses are coordinated with the ventricles.

evidence: A second-degree or incomplete block occurs when some impulses from the SA node reach the AV node and continue, while others do not.

bw: No correlation between atrial and ventricular activity
P waves and QRS complexes independent
tp: In a complete block the AV node or lower tissue paces the ventricles, so there is no link between the P wave and the QRS.

ww.First-degree (partial) AV block: A first-degree block only lengthens the PR interval.
ww.Second-degree (incomplete) AV block: In a second-degree block some P waves are still followed by a QRS complex.

evidence: In the third-degree or complete block, there is no correlation between atrial activity (the P wave) and ventricular activity (the QRS complex).

bw: Area other than the SA node that starts an impulse
May be triggered by ischemia, caffeine or digitalis
tp: Occasional ectopic beats are usually transitory and not life threatening, but chronic ones can lead to arrhythmia or fibrillation.

ww.Bundle branch block: A bundle branch block is an interruption of conduction, not a new impulse source.
ww.Junctional rhythm: Junctional rhythm is a sustained rhythm originating in the AV node, as described for chronic arrhythmias.

evidence: Such an area, which may actually be a component of the conduction system or some other contractile cells, is known as an ectopic focus or ectopic pacemaker.

bw: Ventricles are not effectively pumping blood
Can cause brain death within minutes
tp: With atrial fibrillation the patient may not be in immediate danger as long as the ventricles keep pumping.

ww.Atrial fibrillation: With atrial fibrillation the ventricles continue to pump, so it is not an immediate threat to life.
ww.Third-degree (complete) AV block: A complete block is a conduction block; the source ties life support urgency to ventricular fibrillation.

evidence: Ventricular fibrillation (see Figure 19.25d) is a medical emergency that requires life support, because the ventricles are not effectively pumping blood.

bw: Charge from an external electrical source
Stops the heart so the SA node can restart a normal cycle
tp: External automated defibrillators are placed in schools, restaurants and airports and give simple verbal instructions.

ww.Artificial pacemaker implantation: An artificial pacemaker gives ongoing impulses to the heart muscle to speed up the rate, not a single shock.
ww.Echocardiography: Echocardiography is an ultrasound test of pumping, not a treatment.

evidence: A defibrillator effectively stops the heart so that the SA node can trigger a normal conduction cycle.

bw: Continuously records heart electrical activity for about 24 hours
tp: A Holter records during the patient’s normal routine, unlike a standard electrocardiograph.

ww.Echocardiogram: An echocardiogram is an ultrasound test of pumping effectiveness.
ww.12-lead electrocardiograph: A 12-lead electrocardiograph is the standard instrument, not the portable 24-hour device.

evidence: In continuous ambulatory electrocardiographs, the patient wears a small, portable, battery-operated device known as a Holter monitor, or simply a Holter, that continuously monitors heart electrical activity, typically for a period of 24 hours during the patient’s normal routine.

bw: ST segment elevated above baseline on the ECG
tp: The ST segment may instead appear depressed below baseline when hypoxia is occurring.

ww.Enlargement of the atria: An amplified P wave, not ST elevation, may suggest atrial enlargement.
ww.Myocardial hypoxia: Hypoxia may show ST depression, not elevation.

evidence: An elevation of the ST segment above baseline is often seen in patients with an acute MI, and may appear depressed below the baseline when hypoxia is occurring.

bw: Amplified P wave on an ECG
tp: An enlarged Q wave may indicate a MI, and an enlarged, suppressed or inverted Q wave often indicates enlarged ventricles.

ww.Acute myocardial infarction (MI): MI is linked to an enlarged Q wave and ST elevation.
ww.Enlarged ventricles: Ventricular enlargement is linked to an enlarged, suppressed or inverted Q wave.

evidence: For example, an amplified P wave may indicate enlargement of the atria, an enlarged Q wave may indicate a MI, and an enlarged suppressed or inverted Q wave often indicates enlarged ventricles.

bw: Resting heart rate lower than 50 beats per minute in most people
tp: A few exceptionally trained aerobic athletes have resting rates of 30–40 beats per minute without disease.

ww.Tachycardia: Tachycardia is an abnormally fast rate.
ww.Fibrillation: Fibrillation is uncoordinated beating, not a slow regular rate.

evidence: While a few exceptionally trained aerobic athletes demonstrate resting heart rates in the range of 30–40 beats per minute (the lowest recorded figure is 28 beats per minute for Miguel Indurain, a cyclist), for most individuals, rates lower than 50 beats per minute would indicate a condition called bradycardia.
